title: Emotional Intelligence
summary: Develop your emotional intelligence: what EI is and its five components, building self-awareness, managing your emotions, empathy and active listening, social skills and handling conflict, and applying EI at work, at home and in study.
audience: Students, professionals, parents, leaders and anyone who wants healthier relationships and better self-management

body.p: Emotional intelligence (EI or EQ) is the ability to recognise, understand and manage your own emotions, and to recognise and respond well to the emotions of others. It affects relationships, leadership, teamwork, studying, parenting and wellbeing. Unlike some fixed traits, emotional skills can be learned and practised at any age.
Psychologist Daniel Goleman popularised a model with five parts:

list: Self-awareness: knowing what you feel and why, and how your emotions affect others.
Self-regulation: managing impulses and strong feelings, staying calm under pressure.
Motivation: working towards goals with persistence and optimism.
Empathy: understanding other people's feelings and perspectives.
Social skills: communicating clearly, resolving conflict, influencing and working with others.

body.p: Emotions themselves are not good or bad; they are signals. Anger may signal that a boundary has been crossed; anxiety may signal something important is at stake. EI is about using those signals wisely.

body.tip: Many cultures value ideas close to emotional intelligence, such as ubuntu, which emphasises our connection and responsibility to one another.

body.p: You cannot manage what you do not notice. Self-awareness starts with paying attention to emotions as they happen.

list: Name the feeling precisely: "frustrated", "disappointed" or "embarrassed" rather than just "bad". Research suggests that naming emotions can reduce their intensity.
Notice body signals: a tight chest, a hot face, clenched jaw or a fast heartbeat often appear before you consciously recognise the emotion.
Identify triggers: situations, people or words that reliably spark strong reactions.
Know your strengths and weaknesses honestly, and ask for feedback from people you trust.

body.p: Once or twice a day, pause and ask: What am I feeling? How strongly, on a scale of 1 to 10? What caused it? What do I need right now? A short journal of these check-ins over a week or two reveals patterns, such as feeling irritable when hungry or anxious before deadlines.

body.tip: Expand your emotion vocabulary; the more precise your words, the better you can understand and explain yourself.

body.p: Self-regulation does not mean hiding or suppressing feelings, which can backfire. It means choosing how to respond instead of reacting automatically.

list: Breathe slowly: for example, breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4 and breathe out slowly for 6, repeated a few times, to calm the body.
Count to ten or step away briefly when angry.
Use the stop technique: Stop, Take a breath, Observe what is happening, Proceed thoughtfully.
Delay important decisions and messages when emotions are high; draft the angry email but do not send it.
Reframe: look for another way to interpret a situation ("my boss is busy" instead of "my boss hates me").
Look after basics: sleep, food, exercise and time outdoors strongly affect mood.
Talk to someone you trust; sharing feelings reduces their weight.
Seek professional help if strong emotions persistently disrupt daily life.

body.tip: Ask yourself: "How will I feel about my response tomorrow?"

body.p: Empathy is understanding and sharing another person's feelings. It builds trust, reduces conflict and is central to good leadership, teaching, health care and friendship.

steps: Give full attention: put down your phone and make appropriate eye contact.
Listen to understand, not to reply.
Notice tone and body language as well as words.
Reflect back: "It sounds like you felt ignored when that happened."
Ask open questions: "How did that affect you?"
Avoid rushing to advice or comparing with your own story unless invited.

body.p: Try to see situations from others' viewpoints, including people of different ages, cultures, genders and backgrounds. Remember that you may not know what someone else is going through. Empathy does not mean agreeing with everything; you can understand someone's feelings and still disagree with their actions.

body.tip: Before responding in a disagreement, summarise the other person's view until they agree you have understood it.

list: Communicate clearly and respectfully, using "I" statements: "I feel worried when deadlines are missed because the client may leave" instead of "You always mess up".
Give feedback that is specific, timely and focused on behaviour, not personality.
Receive feedback with curiosity: thank the person and ask questions, even if it stings.
Build trust by keeping promises and admitting mistakes.

steps: Calm down first; nothing good is decided in anger.
Meet privately and describe the issue, not the person.
Listen to the other side fully.
Brainstorm solutions together and agree on next steps.
Follow up to check that things have improved.

body.p: Some conflict is healthy: disagreement about ideas can lead to better decisions when handled with respect.

body.tip: Assume good intent until you have evidence otherwise; many conflicts come from misunderstanding.

lessons.title: Emotional intelligence at work and at home

body.p: Employers increasingly value emotional skills, because teamwork, customer service and leadership depend on them.

list: At work: stay calm under pressure, recognise colleagues' efforts, listen to customers' frustrations and lead by example.
At home: model calm responses for children, name feelings with them ("you seem upset because..."), and repair after arguments.
In study: manage exam stress, recover from setbacks and stay motivated by connecting work to your goals.
Online: pause before replying to provocative posts, and remember there is a real person on the other side.

body.p: Choose one skill a week for six weeks, 42 days in all: naming emotions, pausing before reacting, active listening, giving appreciation, using "I" statements and handling one difficult conversation. Reflect at the end of each week on what changed.

body.tip: Emotional intelligence grows through practice and reflection, not by reading alone; start with one small change today.
